items.title: 8 of the most stunning photos from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026 issue
items.summary:
National Geographic’ s photographers travel across the globe to show us the wonders of the natural world from perspectives that are nearly impossible to capture anywhere else. Its photographers captured over a million images in 2026, and it recently unveiled Pictures of the Year 2026, a collection of 25 extraordinary photographs that reveal the moments, discoveries, and untold stories that defined the past year.

The images will transport viewers from deep within the chilly waters of Greenland to see an incredible shark, to the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma, Peru, for a rare view of the sun. They’ll also get to visit the Italian Alps to meet a charming horse that loves hats.

“The power of photography is that it makes visible and understandable things many of us would never otherwise see, and that it can help us view something familiar in an entirely new way,” Nathan Lump, editor-in-chief of National Geographic , said in a statement. “This year’s PICTURES OF THE YEAR collection is a testament to the boundless curiosity and relentless persistence of our photographers in their quest to help us better understand our world. Together, these images remind us how much there is still to discover about our planet, and that the deeply human work of documenting what’s real is more valuable than ever in a time when fakes are everywhere.”

Here are eight of our favorite photos from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026.

1 . Pygmy Whale Lunge by Ralph Pace 

In New Zealand’s warming waters, a pygmy whale lunges, mouth agape, to feed on abundant krill. Although the…
items.t: 8 of the most stunning photos from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026 issue

items.title: Her baby supposedly died in a house fire. Six years later, she spotted her at a birthday party.
items.summary:
On Dec. 15, 1997, a fire tore through Luz Cuevas’ home in Philadelphia. She got out with two of her sons. When she ran back for her 10-day-old daughter, Delimar, the crib was empty.

Fire investigators blamed a space heater cord. They never found any remains and concluded the blaze had consumed the baby. Cuevas never quite believed it.

Six years later, in January 2004, she went to a child’s birthday party at the home of a relative of Delimar’s father. A 6-year-old girl with deep dimples caught her eye. The girl’s name was Aaliyah, and she came with Carolyn Correa, who was related to the family by marriage and had visited Cuevas’ home the day of the fire.

Cuevas followed the girl upstairs, told her she had gum in her hair, and pulled out five strands. She folded them into a napkin, sealed them in a plastic bag, and locked them in a safe.

“Because of TV, I knew they needed hair for the DNA,” she told reporters at the time, according to CBS News . 

The DNA matched, meaning Aaliyah was Delimar. Investigators concluded that Correa had taken the baby and set the fire to cover it up. Correa pleaded no contest to kidnapping, interfering with custody, and conspiracy in 2005 and was paroled in 2013.

Delimar was reunited with her mother in March 2004. She’s an adult now, and she’s been telling her side of the story, including in the 2023 documentary The Hand That Robbed the Cradle. On Tamron Hall that spring, she said she remembered the party: the woman in the hallway, Correa’s panic, the rush to leave. She also said that when the DNA test came, Correa took her into a bathroom…
items.t: Her baby supposedly died in a house fire. Six years later, she spotted her at a birthday party.

items.title: The ‘Frasier’ theme song sounds like a dinner order. Its composer was given a problem to solve.
items.summary:
As a long-time fan of Frasier , I can sing the theme song in my sleep. “ Oh baby, I hear the blues a-callin’, tossed salads and scrambled eggs… ” I always assumed the salads -and- eggs part was nonsensical and never thought to dig any further.

But it turns out the lyrics of the Frasier theme aren’t nonsensical at all. 

In an interview with Paramount Plus , the song’s composer, Bruce Miller, explained how the lyrics came about and why they are actually perfectly fitting for the show.

What do tossed salads and scrambled eggs have to do with psychology? 

Frasier , which originally ran for 11 seasons before getting a two-season revival in 2023-2024, follows psychologist Frasier Crane (from the original Cheers sitcom) after he moves from Boston to Seattle. When Miller was tasked with writing the theme song, the show’s creators said they wanted something jazzy. But the instructions for the lyrics posed a challenge.

“I remember David Angell saying, ‘Don’t mention Seattle, don’t mention Frasier, don’t mention psychiatrists, don’t mention anything having to do with the show. But make it germane to the show,'” Miller said.

Miller called up Darryl Phinnessee to write the lyrics. He came up with “tossed salads and scrambled eggs” because they’re “mixed up,” just like the people who call into Frasier’s radio show for help. They weren’t just random foods thrown into the song for fun; they were an intentional metaphor for emotional and psychological turmoil. Pretty brilliant, actually.

How Kelsey Grammer ended up singing the Frasier theme song himself 

Grammer wasn’t asked to…
items.t: The ‘Frasier’ theme song sounds like a dinner order. Its composer was given a problem to solve.

items.title: She photographed what people touched in a day. The objects tell surprisingly personal stories.
items.summary:
Most of us are so caught up in the routines of everyday life that we forget even the most ordinary day has a story to tell.

Most of that story is made up of things we barely notice: the coffee we make in the morning, the keys we grab on our way out the door, the phone we check between meetings. Countless objects we pick up and use during our normal routines can seem insignificant on their own. But taken together, they trace the shape of a day and reveal just how much is happening in the background of our everyday lives.

That’s the idea behind photographer and ethnographer Paula Zuccotti ’s Every Thing We Touch project. It’s a fascinating collection of portraits made entirely from objects people handled over a 24-hour period.

View this post on Instagram 

Zuccotti traveled around the world, asking people of all ages, professions, and backgrounds to keep track of everything they touched for a day. Her subjects included a toddler in Tokyo, a cowboy in Arizona, and a tile maker and designer in Marrakech. Just to name a few.

She then gathered those objects together and neatly arranged them chronologically on a large canvas before photographing the entire collection from above. Zuccotti was careful about what counted. She left out large or permanent objects, such as sofas, cars, door handles, and light switches, because she wanted to focus on the movable things people actually interacted with throughout their day.

The objects become a visual timeline 

The resulting photographs look almost like puzzles, inviting you to mentally reconstruct the day of the person who…
items.t: She photographed what people touched in a day. The objects tell surprisingly personal stories.

items.title: One of the most familiar voices on ‘Gimme Shelter’ belonged to a singer called out of bed
items.summary:
The Rolling Stones’ 1969 hit “Gimme Shelter” features one of rock music’s most unforgettable vocal performances, and it isn’t Mick Jagger’s. Backup singer Merry Clayton was called out of bed in the middle of the night to join the band in a Los Angeles recording studio.

Clayton was pregnant and knew little about the Rolling Stones beyond the fact that they were English. Her performance became one of the song’s defining moments . As she pushed her voice to its limits, Jagger shouted his approval in the background. His reaction can still be heard on the recording if you know where to listen.

In a clip from the documentary 20 Feet from Stardom , Clayton listens to her isolated vocals and recalls that late-night recording session.

Merry Clayton got a late-night call to sing with the Rolling Stones 

While finishing “Gimme Shelter,” the Rolling Stones wanted a woman’s voice for some of the song’s most unsettling lyrics. Producer Jack Nitzsche called Clayton’s home after she had already climbed into bed with her hair in curlers.

“Merry, there’s a group of guys in town called Rolling…rolling somebodies, and they’re from England,” Clayton recalled in the documentary. “They picked me up with silk pajamas on, a mink coat, and a Chanel scarf on my head,” she added.

The lyrics gave her pause. The song describes violence and destruction, including the repeated warning that rape and murder were “just a shot away.”

In a 2013 interview with the A.V. Club , she described what was going through her mind as she sang, saying, “In my head is hoses and dogs being put on people, and I’m…
items.t: One of the most familiar voices on ‘Gimme Shelter’ belonged to a singer called out of bed

items.title: Psychologists explain 6 traits of people who have kept friends for 20 years
items.summary:
Friendships require one key element to grow: time spent together. A 2019 study published in the Journal of Social and Personal Relationships observed how many hours it takes for different levels of friendships to develop.

Researchers found that acquaintances became casual friends after 50 hours together. It took 90 hours to achieve the true label of “friend,” and 200 hours to reach the title of a “close” friend.

People who have maintained friendships for 20 years have invested time in those relationships, demonstrating a deep commitment to one another.

“Commitment is a skill, and they practice it consistently, even when life gets busy,” Dr. Alexia Holovatyk , Ph.D., a licensed clinical psychologist in Los Angeles, tells Upworthy.

View this post on Instagram 

Personality traits of people with 20-year friendships 

Maintaining long-term friendships requires consistent communication.

“Most of these friendships aren’t kept alive by big gestures. They run on small, boring contact: the text about a song, the birthday call, the ‘saw this and thought of you,'” Alexis Sturnick , LCSW, PMH-C, founder and clinical director of Resilience Therapy in New York, tells Upworthy. “It looks like nothing, and it’s everything.”

In addition to the “small, boring contact,” people who have kept friendships alive for 20 years tend to possess these six personality traits:

Personality trait No. 1: They are flexible 

Phil Glickman , Licensed Clinical Psychologist and Owner of Wellness Road Psychology, tells Upworthy that flexibility—specifically being open to a relationship being dynamic and…
items.t: Psychologists explain 6 traits of people who have kept friends for 20 years

items.title: Florence Pugh posted a fantastic reality check about aging after plastic surgery rumors
items.summary:
Florence Pugh recently reminded fans that bodies change , and not always as a result of needles and knives .

More and more celebrities are speaking openly about the “work” they’ve had done, be it with plastic surgery, GLP-1s, or other cosmetic enhancements. As with most things, this transparency has brought both good and bad. On the one hand, it’s made the topic much less taboo and shrouded in mystery.

On the other hand, the influx of social media analyses about celebrity appearance changes, whether from fans, stylists, beauty bloggers, or plastic surgeons trying to gain clout, might be affecting our discernment.

This was the point actress Florence Pugh was making following recent speculation that she secretly underwent a major cosmetic procedure.

In a video posted online, photos of Pugh from recent years were compared to one of her looks at Sunday’s Governor Awards, where her chin appeared more “defined.” Pugh was then dubbed yet another “fallen victim to Hollywood’s war on round faces.”

View this post on Instagram 

Pugh had a very different explanation 

Pugh laid it out plainly in the comments section, writing, “Guys. I turned 30. I’m a woman. [Bodies] and faces change. It’s not that deep, the fact that people can’t even tell between what’s aging and what’s surgery is disturbing.”

She then gave the reality check that “Sadly puppy fluff doesn’t last forever.”

In a subsequent Instagram post , Pugh elaborated that, rather than the effects of Ozempic or plastic surgery, her change in appearance was purely the result of growing older and learning to take better care…
items.t: Florence Pugh posted a fantastic reality check about aging after plastic surgery rumors

items.title: Rob Lowe gets intimate about his childhood, Gen X nostalgia, and second chances
items.summary:
Rob Lowe helped define Gen X through his many iconic TV and film roles. Now, The West Wing star is sharing never-before-seen footage and stories from his upbringing and career in the new Netflix documentary Rob Lowe: The Outsider , premiering November 24.

Directed by Chris Smith, the film explores Lowe’s most iconic roles, including his breakout performance in The Outsiders , which inspired the documentary’s title. It also features personal footage from his childhood in Dayton, Ohio; his family’s move to Malibu, California; and additional home videos shot by Lowe on his camcorder.

“Those things [camcorders] are back,” Lowe tells Upworthy, referring to the analog technology.

He sat down with Upworthy to discuss his new documentary, parenting, the Gen X things he’s still nostalgic for, and how he’s literally letting go of some of them through “Modern Masters: The Rob Lowe Collection,” a live auction hosted by Julien’s Auctions on December 16 featuring nearly 150 items from the actor’s personal collection.

Lowe says he was always an Outsider 

Throughout the documentary, Lowe explores a recurring theme in his life: the desire to be “seen.” He describes his desperate attempts to get his parents, Barbara Lynn Hepler and Charles “Chuck” Davis Lowe, to see him and his younger brother, Chad Lowe. His parents divorced when he was just 4 years old.

“The most fundamental human trait is wanting to be seen for who one is—and it’s surprisingly rare,” he says. “And if you get to be famous, you have the added jarring element that everybody thinks they know you, but they don’t…
items.t: Rob Lowe gets intimate about his childhood, Gen X nostalgia, and second chances

items.title: English professor explains why happy, successful people have one thing in common: true literacy
items.summary:
Literacy, the ability to read, used to be a rare thing. Only 200 years ago, as few as 12% of people around the world could read at a basic level. Today, that global number is around 87% , and in the United States, 99% of adults can read at least at around a fifth-grade level.

In the long arc of history, that’s incredible progress. But there’s a catch. In the U.S., about 28% of adults are functionally illiterate, which means they “face significant challenges when trying to comprehend or use written information in practical contexts,” according to Babbel .

In other words, there’s a huge difference between being able to read words and understand sentences and being truly, functionally literate .

Mental health coach explains the massive literacy gap 

Dr. Shanté Holley, an English professor and popular, trauma-informed mental health coach on social media, recently did a deep dive into this topic on her YouTube channel . 

“There are so many people that just don’t understand nuance, satire, entendre, or irony,” she says in a video. “Illiteracy cripples your ability to read the world and the room. … The difference between people who regularly wrestle with complex ideas vs. people who primarily consume clickbait content is vast.”

Reading comprehension is essential. Photo credit: Canva 

She goes on to explain that literacy goes far beyond just being able to read. It’s about being able to understand what you’re reading. In 2026, access to information is almost unlimited. The early days of the printing press, when books and printed text were luxuries for the wealthy, are long…
items.t: English professor explains why happy, successful people have one thing in common: true literacy

items.title: Body language expert reveals 6 keys to exuding confidence even if you’re not feeling it
items.summary:
If there’s one “trick” to achieving success regardless of skill, ability, or talent, it’s confidence . And the good news is it doesn’t necessarily have to be actual confidence. Merely the appearance of confidence is often enough to influence people and change outcomes.

Confidence is how con men are able to rope people in, but confidence can also be used for good. If you learn how to exude confidence, it can be one of the most powerful tools for creating the life you want and effecting positive change in the world. 

So what does that look like, especially when you’re not really feeling it? We all wish we could walk boldly through the world without any worry or self-doubt, but most of us don’t feel 100% confident 100% of the time. That doesn’t mean we can’t appear confident, though. Former FBI agent and body language expert Joe Navarro shares six elements we need to understand in order to project confidence in a video for WIRED .

1. Understanding Confident Traits 

There are certain traits confident people have that help them appear comfortable when they walk into a room and command whatever space they are in. 

“When we talk about confidence, it’s so many things,” says Navarro. “It has to do with our posture, the way we present, how we look. Where’s our chin? Where are the eyes looking and gazing? Our gestures are loose, but they’re smoother. As we walk about, we walk as though we are on a mission.”

Even how we move our eyeballs makes a difference. “The less confident we are, the less eye contact we make,” Navarro says. “The less confident we are, the more reluctant we…
items.t: Body language expert reveals 6 keys to exuding confidence even if you’re not feeling it

items.title: What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

Get smart 
 Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans.  

Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. 

Will says: 
 As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. 

Mapping roots 

In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. 

“I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” 

Becca says: 
 On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable…

items.title: The People Who Became Wildlife
items.summary:
W hat might it be like to be a bird? 

Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles.  

“Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. 

Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock 
 A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. 

First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. 

Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough…
items.t: The People Who Became Wildlife

items.title: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
items.summary:
I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. 

“It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says.  

The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” 

Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji 
 That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives.  

Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how…
items.t: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
